# drops

A cross-project issue tracker for AI coding agents. Go, pure-Go SQLite, and
Cobra; one database for every repository, with the project resolved from the
working directory.

**Read [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md) before working here.** It carries the gate, the
scratch-store rule, the test discipline every ticket is held to, and the tools in
this environment that report success while failing.

Issues live in **GitHub Issues** on
[`tedkulp/drops`](https://github.com/tedkulp/drops), driven by the `gh` CLI —
not in the `drops` store this repo builds. `docs/agents/issue-tracker.md` is the
contract for working them; the open queue there is the work queue, and
checked-in notes are not a parallel plan.

The `dw32p` rewrite map that carried this repo to 0.2.0 is closed. Its 79 issues
stay in `~/.drops/drops.db`, which is why `dw32p.N` ids appear in `CHANGELOG.md`
and `docs/research/`.

# Working in drops

A cross-project issue tracker for AI coding agents. Go, pure-Go SQLite, and Cobra;
one database for every repository, with the project resolved from the working
directory.

## Agent skills

### Issue tracker

GitHub Issues on `tedkulp/drops`, driven by the `gh` CLI. See
[docs/agents/issue-tracker.md](docs/agents/issue-tracker.md); its **Wayfinding
operations** section defines how to work a map. Issues do **not** live in the
`drops` store any more — that history is closed and stays where it is.

### Triage labels

The five canonical roles, each label string equal to its name. See
[docs/agents/triage-labels.md](docs/agents/triage-labels.md).

### Domain docs

Single-context: `CONTEXT.md` at the root, ADRs under `docs/adr/` once there are
any. See [docs/agents/domain.md](docs/agents/domain.md).

### Which skill for what

`codebase-design` for package shape and seams, `tdd` for build tickets, `grilling`
plus `domain-modeling` for decision tickets.

## The gate

`just test-all`: `go vet` and a gofmt check, then `go test ./... -race`. A green
`go test` is not a green build.

CI runs this **recipe**, not a copy of it. `.github/workflows/ci.yml` installs
`just` and calls `just test-all`, because a workflow that wrote the steps out
would be a second gate free to drift from this one — and a hand-rolled `go test`
step would drop the `DROPS_DB` tripwire below without saying so. `release_test.go`
holds the workflow to the recipe. A second CI job runs `goreleaser check`, so a
broken `.goreleaser.yaml` is found on a push rather than on a tag.

The gofmt check formats what **git** counts as part of this tree — tracked files
plus untracked ones git would offer to add — and not everything under `.`. So an
unformatted `.go` file left in the gitignored `/.scratch/` does not fail the gate,
while a new file you have not run `git add` on still does. "What git counts" means
git's whole exclude set, not `.gitignore` alone: `.git/info/exclude` and your
`core.excludesFile` are read too, so the gate's view of this tree is exactly `git
status`'s view, and the untracked half of that is as machine-specific as `git
status` is. Tracked files are not — `--cached` ignores excludes.

The vet half has the mirror-image trap, and the gate now covers it. `./...` is
not every package in this tree: the go tool drops `testdata` directories from
that pattern, and any directory whose name begins with `.` or `_`. So
`internal/lockfile/testdata/holder` — the real second process the lockfile
contention tests build and run, not sample data — was formatted but never
vetted. The gate vets those packages by path, and the set is **derived** as the
directories git counts minus the ones `go list ./...` reports, rather than by
naming `testdata`, so a helper added under any skipped directory is vetted on
arrival. Directories under a nested `go.mod` are excluded, because `go vet`
refuses a path in another module and `tools/mutate/testdata/fixture` is a
deliberately-mutated corpus for the mutate tool's own tests.

`test` and `mutate` export `DROPS_DB` to `/dev/null/no-default-store-in-tests/drops.db`
— not a scratch store but a tripwire, so a test that reaches for `store.DefaultPath()`
fails with ENOTDIR and names the path. Since the cutover (`dw32p.28`) this is the
**only** thing between a test and the real store: the binary this repository builds
owns `~/.drops/drops.db`, so `internal/store`'s development guard is gone and nothing
in runtime code refuses that path any more. Issues live in the store the suite must
never open.

Four tools lie about success here:

- `gofmt -l` exits zero while listing files. The file list is the signal, never `$?`.
- `grep -c` exits one on zero matches and silently skips the rest of an `&&` chain.
- `go test` prints `ok` for a package whose tests all skipped. Read the skip count
  and the test events before treating that output as proof.
- `go run` exits 1 whatever its program exited, printing `exit status 3` to stderr.
  A recipe that needs the program's own exit code must `go build` and run the binary.

## Test discipline

The dominant defect in this codebase is a test that appears to cover a requirement
but **cannot fail for it**. Coverage does not detect it: `render` and `resolve` sit
at 100% function coverage and mutation still found defects in both. Annotated
red-checks found zero holes across the reference build; unannotated mutation found
every one.

So the standard is not a number. It is that each requirement has a **control** — the
production branch that makes it true — and that control has been mutated with the
test observed **red**.

### Which controls get mutated

One per **requirement clause**: a behavioural claim the ticket's question names. Not
one per test function — that turns the count into the goal and selects for cheap
mutations.

Where a clause is too coarse to mutate in one place, split it by **load-bearing
branch**: parsers, orderings, comparisons, conflict resolution, guards, refusals.
Those are where a wrong implementation still passes. A struct that round-trips does
not need a control; a comparator does.

### How a mutation is run

`just mutate`. The four steps are the recipe's, not yours:

1. Snapshot the file and record its checksum.
2. Apply the mutation.
3. Run the one named test, expecting failure. A pass is the finding: the test does
   not cover the clause — fix the test, not the record.
4. Restore from the snapshot and verify the checksum matches.

The snapshot is harness-owned, so **you no longer have to commit first**. `git
checkout` was never the restore here — a restore command cannot distinguish a
mutation from uncommitted work — and the harness never runs one. A run killed
between steps 2 and 4 leaves a journal naming exactly what to put back; the next
run refuses to start, and `just mutate --restore` finishes it.

Controls live beside the code they mutate, in each package's `mutations.json`: a
name, the requirement clause it proves, the file, the `old` → `new` edit, and the
test. `just mutate` runs every one; `just mutate core` scopes to a package or a
single control name; `--list` prints what is catalogued without running it; and
`--file/--old/--new/--test/--clause` runs one ad hoc, for while you are still
finding out whether a test can fail at all.

It refuses more than it accepts, and every refusal is a finding, never a pass:

| It says | It means |
|---|---|
| `GREEN` | the test passed with the branch broken, so it does not cover the clause |
| `NOT RUN` | no test of that name ran — `go test -run` matching nothing prints `ok` and exits 0 |
| `BUILD FAILED` | the mutation does not compile, so it proves nothing about the test |
| `NO MATCH` | `old` is absent or appears twice; a mutation must name exactly one branch |
| `BASELINE RED` | the test was already failing, so its red says nothing |

Exit 0 means every control went red, 1 that there is a finding, 2 that it was
called wrong, and **3 that a restore failed and the tree may still hold a
mutation**.

`just mutate` is deliberately not part of `test-all`. The gate asks whether this
commit is green; mutation asks whether the suite can fail, and pays a compile per
control to answer. Run it when a ticket adds or changes a control.

### What a ticket records

Enumerate, in `close --reason`: each control (file and behaviour), the test that went
red, and confirmation of the restore. `just mutate <package>` prints exactly that, so
the enumeration is a by-product rather than prose written from memory, and `--json` is
the same record for a machine. A bare count is unauditable — it is the form that let a
ticket record "one control" without anyone reading it as "one".

A control that is not in a `mutations.json` was proved once and can never be proved
again. Catalogue it.

### Seams

**Discovered facts become constructor parameters; real subsystems stay real.**

A fact a process learns about its environment — the writer, terminal-ness, measured
width, the pager, the clock, the ID source — is a struct field passed in, never
discovered at the point of use. `render` accepts all four of its environment facts,
so its whole suite is byte-exact literals with no fake anywhere; the reference build
discovered them and needed two package-level variables to make the same behaviour
reachable.

The datastore is not such a fact. There is deliberately no `Store` interface: every
test runs against real temp SQLite, real git, and real `flock`. `synctest` cannot
fake SQLite's busy-handler sleep, so lock-contention tests are real-clock. Making
these fakeable would trade a real defect class for a faster suite.

### Serialized contracts

For at least one case per serialized contract, run the real writer and decode its
bytes. Deriving both sides from the same description tests the description.

### The CLI is a contract

`docs/cli-contract.md` is what agents read to drive drops. A verb that
changes shape without that file changing is a defect.

Every command in the tree carries at least one boundary test through
`RunForTest(args, db, cwd)`, asserting what the doc says a reader observes: a
byte-exact row for a scanning verb, the JSON shape for a reading verb, the store
effect for a mutating verb. A census test walks the command tree and fails on any
command absent from the tested-verb registry, so skipping one is an edit to a visible
list rather than an omission.

## Changelog

`CHANGELOG.md` follows Keep a Changelog. Every change made after the latest
release goes under `## [Unreleased]` (create it when absent), grouped under the
appropriate change category. Only release work moves those entries into a dated
version section.

## Lessons retained from the reference build

- Re-check the premise before the next round of rigour, not after it.
- Measure before changing a documented fact. A confidently wrong count is worse than
  a stale one.

## Planning

This repository has no `.internal/` tree. Durable research belongs in `docs/`; live
plans and decisions belong in the issue tracker. The local `.gitignore` deliberately
overrides the workstation's global `.internal/` exclusion so accidental files cannot
disappear from status.
# Issue tracker: GitHub

Issues and specs for this repo live as GitHub issues in
[`tedkulp/drops`](https://github.com/tedkulp/drops). Use the `gh` CLI for all
operations; run it inside a clone and it infers the repo from `git remote -v`.

> **This repo builds a tracker but does not use it as one.** Until 2026-09-06 the
> issues for this repo lived in `drops` itself. That history — 79 closed issues,
> including the `dw32p` rewrite map — stays in `~/.drops/drops.db` under the
> `drops` project and is not migrated; the `dw32p.N` ids cited in `CHANGELOG.md`
> and `docs/research/*.md` refer to it. Nothing is open there. For how the
> product's own CLI behaves, see [docs/cli-contract.md](../cli-contract.md).

## Conventions

- **Create an issue**: `gh issue create --title "..." --body "..."`. Use a heredoc for multi-line bodies.
- **Read an issue**: `gh issue view <number> --comments`, filtering comments by `jq` and also fetching labels.
- **List issues**: `gh issue list --state open --json number,title,body,labels,comments --jq '[.[] | {number, title, body, labels: [.labels[].name], comments: [.comments[].body]}]'` with appropriate `--label` and `--state` filters.
- **Comment on an issue**: `gh issue comment <number> --body "..."`
- **Apply / remove labels**: `gh issue edit <number> --add-label "..."` / `--remove-label "..."`
- **Close**: `gh issue close <number> --comment "..."`

## Pull requests as a triage surface

**PRs as a request surface: no.** _(Set to `yes` if this repo treats external PRs as feature requests; `/triage` reads this flag.)_

When set to `yes`, PRs run through the same labels and states as issues, using the `gh pr` equivalents:

- **Read a PR**: `gh pr view <number> --comments` and `gh pr diff <number>` for the diff.
- **List external PRs for triage**: `gh pr list --state open --json number,title,body,labels,author,authorAssociation,comments` then keep only `authorAssociation` of `CONTRIBUTOR`, `FIRST_TIME_CONTRIBUTOR`, or `NONE` (drop `OWNER`/`MEMBER`/`COLLABORATOR`).
- **Comment / label / close**: `gh pr comment`, `gh pr edit --add-label`/`--remove-label`, `gh pr close`.

GitHub shares one number space across issues and PRs, so a bare `#42` may be either: resolve with `gh pr view 42` and fall back to `gh issue view 42`.

## When a skill says "publish to the issue tracker"

Create a GitHub issue.

## When a skill says "fetch the relevant ticket"

Run `gh issue view <number> --comments`.

## Wayfinding operations

Used by `/wayfinder`. The **map** is a single issue with **child** issues as tickets.

- **Map**: a single issue labelled `wayfinder:map`, holding the Notes / Decisions-so-far / Fog body. `gh issue create --label wayfinder:map`.
- **Child ticket**: an issue linked to the map as a GitHub sub-issue (`gh api` on the sub-issues endpoint). Where sub-issues aren't enabled, add the child to a task list in the map body and put `Part of #<map>` at the top of the child body. Labels: `wayfinder:<type>` (`research`/`prototype`/`grilling`/`task`). Once claimed, the ticket is assigned to the driving dev.
- **Blocking**: GitHub's **native issue dependencies**, the canonical, UI-visible representation. Add an edge with `gh api --method POST repos/<owner>/<repo>/issues/<child>/dependencies/blocked_by -F issue_id=<blocker-db-id>`, where `<blocker-db-id>` is the blocker's numeric **database id** (`gh api repos/<owner>/<repo>/issues/<n> --jq .id`, _not_ the `#number` or `node_id`). GitHub reports `issue_dependencies_summary.blocked_by` (open blockers only, the live gate). Where dependencies aren't available, fall back to a `Blocked by: #<n>, #<n>` line at the top of the child body. A ticket is unblocked when every blocker is closed.
- **Frontier query**: list the map's open children (`gh issue list --state open`, scoped to the map's sub-issues / task list), drop any with an open blocker (`issue_dependencies_summary.blocked_by > 0`, or an open issue in the `Blocked by` line) or an assignee; first in map order wins.
- **Claim**: `gh issue edit <n> --add-assignee @me`, the session's first write.
- **Resolve**: `gh issue comment <n> --body "<answer>"`, then `gh issue close <n>`, then append a context pointer (gist + link) to the map's Decisions-so-far.

Controls live beside the code they mutate, in each package's `mutations.json`: a
name, the requirement clause it proves, the file, the `old` → `new` edit, and the
test. `just mutate` runs every one; `just mutate core` scopes to a package or a
single control name; `--list` prints what is catalogued without running it; and
`--file/--old/--new/--test/--clause` runs one ad hoc, for while you are still
finding out whether a test can fail at all.

It refuses more than it accepts, and every refusal is a finding, never a pass:

| It says | It means |
|---|---|
| `GREEN` | the test passed with the branch broken, so it does not cover the clause |
| `NOT RUN` | no test of that name ran — `go test -run` matching nothing prints `ok` and exits 0 |
| `BUILD FAILED` | the mutation does not compile, so it proves nothing about the test |
| `NO MATCH` | `old` is absent or appears twice; a mutation must name exactly one branch |
| `BASELINE RED` | the test was already failing, so its red says nothing |

Exit 0 means every control went red, 1 that there is a finding, 2 that it was
called wrong, and **3 that a restore failed and the tree may still hold a
mutation**.

`just mutate` is deliberately not part of `test-all`. The gate asks whether this
commit is green; mutation asks whether the suite can fail, and pays a compile per
control to answer. Run it when a ticket adds or changes a control.

### What a ticket records

Enumerate, in `close --reason`: each control (file and behaviour), the test that went
red, and confirmation of the restore. `just mutate <package>` prints exactly that, so
the enumeration is a by-product rather than prose written from memory, and `--json` is
the same record for a machine. A bare count is unauditable — it is the form that let a
ticket record "one control" without anyone reading it as "one".

A control that is not in a `mutations.json` was proved once and can never be proved
again. Catalogue it.

### Seams

**Discovered facts become constructor parameters; real subsystems stay real.**

A fact a process learns about its environment — the writer, terminal-ness, measured
width, the pager, the clock, the ID source — is a struct field passed in, never
discovered at the point of use. `render` accepts all four of its environment facts,
so its whole suite is byte-exact literals with no fake anywhere; the reference build
discovered them and needed two package-level variables to make the same behaviour
reachable.

The datastore is not such a fact. There is deliberately no `Store` interface: every
test runs against real temp SQLite, real git, and real `flock`. `synctest` cannot
fake SQLite's busy-handler sleep, so lock-contention tests are real-clock. Making
these fakeable would trade a real defect class for a faster suite.

### Serialized contracts

For at least one case per serialized contract, run the real writer and decode its
bytes. Deriving both sides from the same description tests the description.

### The CLI is a contract

`docs/cli-contract.md` is what agents read to drive drops. A verb that
changes shape without that file changing is a defect.

Every command in the tree carries at least one boundary test through
`RunForTest(args, db, cwd)`, asserting what the doc says a reader observes: a
byte-exact row for a scanning verb, the JSON shape for a reading verb, the store
effect for a mutating verb. A census test walks the command tree and fails on any
command absent from the tested-verb registry, so skipping one is an edit to a visible
list rather than an omission.

`CHANGELOG.md` follows Keep a Changelog. Every change made after the latest

Issues and specs for this repo live as GitHub issues in
[`tedkulp/drops`](https://github.com/tedkulp/drops). Use the `gh` CLI for all

## Conventions

- **Create an issue**: `gh issue create --title "..." --body "..."`. Use a heredoc for multi-line bodies.
- **Read an issue**: `gh issue view <number> --comments`, filtering comments by `jq` and also fetching labels.
- **List issues**: `gh issue list --state open --json number,title,body,labels,comments --jq '[.[] | {number, title, body, labels: [.labels[].name], comments: [.comments[].body]}]'` with appropriate `--label` and `--state` filters.
- **Comment on an issue**: `gh issue comment <number> --body "..."`
- **Apply / remove labels**: `gh issue edit <number> --add-label "..."` / `--remove-label "..."`
- **Close**: `gh issue close <number> --comment "..."`

## Pull requests as a triage surface

**PRs as a request surface: no.** _(Set to `yes` if this repo treats external PRs as feature requests; `/triage` reads this flag.)_

When set to `yes`, PRs run through the same labels and states as issues, using the `gh pr` equivalents:

- **Read a PR**: `gh pr view <number> --comments` and `gh pr diff <number>` for the diff.
- **List external PRs for triage**: `gh pr list --state open --json number,title,body,labels,author,authorAssociation,comments` then keep only `authorAssociation` of `CONTRIBUTOR`, `FIRST_TIME_CONTRIBUTOR`, or `NONE` (drop `OWNER`/`MEMBER`/`COLLABORATOR`).
- **Comment / label / close**: `gh pr comment`, `gh pr edit --add-label`/`--remove-label`, `gh pr close`.

GitHub shares one number space across issues and PRs, so a bare `#42` may be either: resolve with `gh pr view 42` and fall back to `gh issue view 42`.

## When a skill says "publish to the issue tracker"

Create a GitHub issue.

## When a skill says "fetch the relevant ticket"

Run `gh issue view <number> --comments`.

## Wayfinding operations

Used by `/wayfinder`. The **map** is a single issue with **child** issues as tickets.

- **Map**: a single issue labelled `wayfinder:map`, holding the Notes / Decisions-so-far / Fog body. `gh issue create --label wayfinder:map`.
- **Child ticket**: an issue linked to the map as a GitHub sub-issue (`gh api` on the sub-issues endpoint). Where sub-issues aren't enabled, add the child to a task list in the map body and put `Part of #<map>` at the top of the child body. Labels: `wayfinder:<type>` (`research`/`prototype`/`grilling`/`task`). Once claimed, the ticket is assigned to the driving dev.
- **Blocking**: GitHub's **native issue dependencies**, the canonical, UI-visible representation. Add an edge with `gh api --method POST repos/<owner>/<repo>/issues/<child>/dependencies/blocked_by -F issue_id=<blocker-db-id>`, where `<blocker-db-id>` is the blocker's numeric **database id** (`gh api repos/<owner>/<repo>/issues/<n> --jq .id`, _not_ the `#number` or `node_id`). GitHub reports `issue_dependencies_summary.blocked_by` (open blockers only, the live gate). Where dependencies aren't available, fall back to a `Blocked by: #<n>, #<n>` line at the top of the child body. A ticket is unblocked when every blocker is closed.
- **Frontier query**: list the map's open children (`gh issue list --state open`, scoped to the map's sub-issues / task list), drop any with an open blocker (`issue_dependencies_summary.blocked_by > 0`, or an open issue in the `Blocked by` line) or an assignee; first in map order wins.
- **Claim**: `gh issue edit <n> --add-assignee @me`, the session's first write.
- **Resolve**: `gh issue comment <n> --body "<answer>"`, then `gh issue close <n>`, then append a context pointer (gist + link) to the map's Decisions-so-far.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

Spec for board v1, from the map [Kanban board in the TUI](https://github.com/tedkulp/drops/issues/1). Its decisions come from the closed tickets #2, #3, #4, #5, and #6. The look comes from the prototype on branch [`prototype/board-look`](https://github.com/tedkulp/drops/tree/prototype/board-look) (`1e0cd38`, variant E, 3-line cards).

## Problem Statement

`drops tui` shows one scope as a flat list, in the CLI's order. To see where the work stands (what can be picked up, what is waiting on something, what is under way, and what just finished), a person has to switch `r` and `C` on and off and hold the rest in their head. The list marks a blocked row with ` [N]` but cannot group rows by where they are in the flow. It also hides closed work unless `C` is on, and then mixes it in with live rows. Moving an issue along the flow means opening `x` and picking a verb, and there is no one motion that says "I'm starting this".

## Solution

A **board** view inside `drops tui`. `B` switches between the list and the board. The board sets out the live issues in scope in four derived **Board columns** (Ready | Blocked | In progress | Closed), one card per issue, with the detail pane still on screen to the right. `tab`/`shift+tab` moves between columns. Every existing key keeps its meaning. `m` moves a card by changing its status, using the flows the navigator already has for closing and reopening. Moving a card into In progress also claims it if nobody holds the claim, in one write.

At narrow widths the board shows as many columns as fit, each at least 28 wide, and scrolls sideways to keep the focused column on screen. Polling, the stale marker, follow, `x`, and `y` work as they do in the list.

## User Stories

**Entering, leaving, and what carries over**

1. As a person at a terminal, I want `B` to switch `drops tui` between the list and the board, so that I can see the flow without leaving the navigator.
2. As a person, I want `drops tui` to always open in the list, so that starting it behaves as it did before the board.
3. As a person, I want the issue under my cursor to stay the cursor's issue when I press `B`, so that switching views doesn't lose my place.
4. As a person, I want my `/` filter, `a` scope, `r` narrowing, and follow trail to carry over when I press `B`, so that the board narrows to what the list was narrowed to.
5. As a person, I want `B` to read nothing from the store, so that switching views is instant and the rows don't change under me.
6. As a person, I want `Esc` not to leave the board, so that a stray `Esc` while backing out of a picker or filter doesn't drop me into the list.
7. As a person who uses `b` to page the detail pane up, I want `b` to keep doing that, so that the board key doesn't take a key I already use.

**Columns**

8. As a person, I want open issues with no unfinished blocker in **Ready**, so that I can see what can be picked up.
9. As a person, I want open issues with at least one unfinished blocker in **Blocked**, so that I can see what is waiting.
10. As a person, I want every `in_progress` issue in **In progress**, even a blocked one, so that started work never looks unstarted.
11. As a person, I want a blocked In progress card to say `blocked by N`, so that I can see started work that is stuck.
12. As a person, I want closed issues in **Closed**, always shown whatever `C` is set to, so that recently finished work is on the board.
13. As a person, I want Closed ordered most recently closed first, so that the top of the column is what just finished.
14. As a person, I want Ready, Blocked, and In progress in the CLI's order (priority, newest, id), so that the board and `drops list` agree.
15. As a person, I want no manual ranking, so that priority stays the one ordering tool.
16. As a person, I want tombstoned issues never to appear on the board, so that removed work doesn't clutter it.

**Cards**

17. As a person, I want line 1 of a card to show the status mark, `P<n>`, type, and id, with age right-aligned, so that I can identify a card at a glance.
18. As a person, I want a card's age measured from when it was created (Ready and Blocked), started (In progress), or closed (Closed), so that the age means something in each column.
19. As a person, I want line 2 to be the title, cut with an ellipsis, so that long titles don't break the column.
20. As a person, I want line 3 to show `@assignee · blocked by N · unblocks N · #label #label`, with each part only when present, so that I see who holds it, what it waits on, what it frees, and how it's tagged, without empty placeholders.
21. As a person, I want a card's labels to be its live labels only, so that removed labels don't show.
22. As a person, I want one blank line between cards and the focused card in reverse video, so that cards read as separate and I can see which is selected.

**Layout and width**

23. As a person, I want the detail pane to stay on screen at 40% of the frame (at least 38 columns), so that the page for the focused card is always readable.
24. As a person on an 80-column terminal, I want one full-width column at a time rather than four unreadable slivers, so that cards stay legible.
25. As a person at 120 columns, I want two columns, and at 200 columns all four, so that wider terminals show more of the board.
26. As a person, I want the board border to say how many columns are hidden on each side (e.g. `◀ 1 · 1 ▶`), so that I know there is more off screen.
27. As a person, I want `tab`/`shift+tab` to scroll the board sideways when the target column is off screen, so that the focused column is always visible.
28. As a person, I want the focused column's heading marked with `▸`, so that I know which column my keys act on.
29. As a person, I want each heading to show the column's name and count, so that I can see column sizes without scrolling.

**Long and empty columns**

30. As a person, I want a column longer than the screen to scroll a card at a time and keep the cursor's card on screen, so that I never lose the selected card.
31. As a person, I want an overflowing column's heading to show the visible range (e.g. `Closed 300 · 39–41`), so that I know where I am in a long column.
32. As a person, I want an empty column to keep its heading and show a dim hint (`none`, or `nothing closed` for Closed), so that an empty column reads as empty rather than broken.

**Movement**

33. As a person, I want `j` `k` `↓` `↑` `g` `G` `^d` `^u` to move within the focused column, so that movement matches the list.
34. As a person, I want `tab` and `shift+tab` to cycle through the four columns and wrap around, so that I can reach any column from any other.
35. As a person, I want `tab` to land on the card nearest my old row position, so that moving sideways keeps my place on screen.
36. As a person, I want moving the card cursor to clear the follow trail, as moving the list cursor does, so that the trail always belongs to the cursor's issue.
37. As a person, I want `h` `l` `←` `→` `0` `$` `J` `K` `space` `b` `w` `enter` `f` `Backspace` `x` `y` to act on the detail pane as they do in the list, so that I don't learn a second keymap.

**Narrowings**

38. As a person, I want `/` to filter the cards in every column, so that filtering works the same in both views.
39. As a person, I want `r` on the board to use the same ready-only predicate as the list, so that "ready" means one thing.
40. As a person, I want Blocked to show `r to show blocked` while `r` is on, so that I know why it's empty and how to get it back.
41. As a person, I want `r` to hide blocked In progress cards too, so that `r` consistently shows only unblocked work.
42. As a person, I want `C` on the board to show the notice `closed always shown on the board`, cleared by the next key, so that I know the key did nothing on purpose.
43. As a person, I want `C` on the board to leave the list's `C` setting alone, so that switching back with `B` gives me the list as I left it.

**Moving cards**

44. As a person, I want `m` to open a picker, like the `x` modal, over the statuses the card could move to, so that moving a card is one key and one choice.
45. As a person, I want the picker to leave out the card's current status, so that every row changes something.
46. As a person, I want Ready and Blocked to appear as one `open` row, so that I'm not offered a column the card might not land in.
47. As a person, I want a card moved to `open` to land in whichever of Ready or Blocked its readiness puts it, so that columns stay derived.
48. As a person, I want a status line (e.g. `open — blocked by 2`) when a card moved to `open` lands in Blocked, so that I know why it didn't land in Ready.
49. As a person, I want moving a card into In progress to claim it for me if nobody holds the claim, so that starting work and taking it are one motion.
50. As a person, I want moving into In progress to leave someone else's claim alone and still succeed, so that I can mark work started without taking it from its owner.
51. As a person, I want `started_at` set only the first time an issue enters In progress, so that the start date isn't reset by moving a card back and forth.
52. As a person, I want moving out of In progress never to release the claim, so that a move never drops ownership by accident (`x release` still does that).
53. As a person, I want moving a card to `closed` to open the same `$EDITOR` flow as `x close`, so that every close has a written reason.
54. As a person, I want an empty or whitespace-only reason, or a non-zero editor exit, to cancel the close and leave the card where it was, so that I can back out.
55. As a person, I want closing not to touch the claim, so that the claim records who resolved the issue.
56. As a person, I want moving a card out of Closed to ask the same y/N as `reopen`, including how many characters of close reason will be lost, so that I don't lose a reason by accident.
57. As a person, I want no prompt when a closed issue has no close reason, so that there's no confirmation when nothing is lost.
58. As a person, I want any answer but `y` to leave the card in Closed, so that a stray key never reopens anything.
59. As a person, I want moving a card from Closed to In progress to ask the reopen question and then claim if unclaimed, so that both rules apply in order.

**After a write or refresh**

60. As a person, I want the cursor to follow a moved card into whichever column it lands in, so that I can keep acting on it.
61. As a person, I want the cursor, if the card leaves the view (tombstoned, filtered out, or hidden by `r`), to go to the next card in its column, else the previous one, else the nearest non-empty column, so that I always land somewhere sensible.
62. As a person, I want the detail pane to open the new card at line 0 when the cursor lands on a different issue, so that the board follows the navigator's different-issue rule.
63. As a person, I want a cancelled close or a declined reopen to write nothing and leave the cursor where it was, so that backing out has no effect.
64. As a person, I want the `write_seq` poll and the `stale · R` footer marker to work on the board as they do in the list, so that I notice other writers without the board reordering under me.
65. As a person, I want `R` to refresh whichever view is up, so that refreshing works the same in both.
66. As a person, I want a move to write with last-write-wins semantics, like every `x` write, so that the board adds no new conflict rules.

**Help and documentation**

67. As a person, I want `?` to list `B`, `tab`, and `m`, so that I can find the board keys in the navigator.
68. As an agent reading `docs/cli-contract.md`, I want the board described in its own subsection of the navigator section, so that the contract covers every surface drops ships.
69. As an agent, I want Known rough edges to say that Closed loads with no limit and a refresh costs about 100ms at around 10k closed issues, so that a slow board on a large store isn't mistaken for a bug.

**Performance**

70. As a person with a store of about 1,000 issues, I want a board refresh to stay around 10ms, so that `R` and post-write refreshes feel as fast as the list's.
71. As a person, I want one board refresh to read the blocker graph once, so that the board doesn't pay for `OpenBlockers` twice.

## Implementation Decisions

**Domain vocabulary.** Use **Board column**, **Ready issue**, **Blocked issue**, **Open issue**, **Live issue**, and **Deferral** as `CONTEXT.md` defines them. The **Board column** entry is part of this effort, so commit it if it is still uncommitted. A column is derived, never stored. A deferred issue is an ordinary open issue on the board.

**Where it lives.** Board mode is part of `internal/tui`, not a separate command. It replaces the left pane and reuses the navigator's detail pane, follow stack, `x`, `y`, poll, and stale marker. `internal/cli` doesn't change: there is no new verb or flag, and `tui` is already in the census.

**Core: four changes before the TUI work** (#3, #4). Pick each exact name and signature with `codebase-design`.

1. **Start-and-claim write.** One transaction and one revision that sets `in_progress`, sets `started_at` only if it is unset, and sets the assignee to the given author only if the issue is unclaimed. It never refuses because someone else holds the claim. It keeps core's refusal of tombstoned issues. There is no CLI verb for it.
2. **Closed-issues read, scoped.** Closed live issues in the project scope, or in all projects under `a`, ordered in the store by `closed_at DESC, id`. Tombstoned issues are excluded. No limit in v1, and it stays a separate read so a limit can be added later as one parameter.
3. **Blocker-graph read.** Blocked-by counts and unblock (downstream) counts from one read of the blocker graph. Either one call returns both, or `UnblockImpacts` accepts the blocker map the caller already has. The "only this blocker" downstream rule stays in core. The TUI never computes it.
4. **Live-labels read, store-wide.** Returns a map from issue id to that issue's live label names, sorted. No scope, like `OpenBlockers`. It uses its own live-only store query, not a filter over the export read `Labels()`. The TUI must not read labels per card.

Every other move uses `SetIssueStatus` unchanged: `open`, and `closed` with a reason.

**One board refresh makes four reads:** the existing open and in-progress `Issues` read (in the CLI's order), the closed-issues read, the blocker-graph read, and the live-labels read. Measured at 8.8ms on a 1,031-issue store. The TUI never re-sorts rows: Closed's order comes from core. The poll still reads only `write_seq`. The board loads closed issues whatever `C` is set to. The list's `C` setting is kept separately.

**Column derivation** (one branch each): `open` with no open blocker → Ready; `open` with an open blocker → Blocked; `in_progress` → In progress, blocked or not; `closed` → Closed.

**Keymap** (#5)

| key | on the board |
|---|---|
| `B` | switch between list and board (reads nothing; carries the cursor id, `/`, `a`, `r`, and the follow trail) |
| `tab` / `shift+tab` | next / previous column, wrapping around all four; land on the nearest row position; scroll the board sideways to show the target |
| `j` `k` `↓` `↑` `g` `G` `^d` `^u` | move within the focused column; clears the follow trail |
| `m` | move picker: `open` / `in progress` / `closed`, minus the card's own status |
| `r` | the same `blockedBy == 0` predicate in `applyFilter`; Blocked empties with `r to show blocked`, and blocked In progress cards are hidden |
| `C` | notice `closed always shown on the board`, cleared on the next key; changes no state |
| `Esc` | pops layers as it does in the list; never leaves the board |
| all others | unchanged |

**Move flows** (#3)

- `m` → `open`: `SetIssueStatus(open)`. When the card lands in Blocked, the status line says `open — blocked by N`.
- `m` → `in progress`: the start-and-claim write, never `SetIssueStatus`.
- `m` → `closed`: the existing `x close` `$EDITOR` flow. An empty or whitespace-only reason, or a non-zero exit, writes nothing.
- Any move out of Closed first runs the existing `reopen` y/N, but only when there is a close reason to lose. Anything but `y` writes nothing. A move to In progress then follows the start-and-claim rule.
- Moves never release a claim. There is no revision guard. Tombstoned issues are never shown, and core's existing tombstone refusal covers one tombstoned while it is on screen.

**Cursor after a write or refresh.** The cursor rides its tracked id into whichever column the card lands in. If the id has left the view, it goes to the next card in the same column, else the previous one, else the nearest non-empty column. The detail pane then follows the existing rule: same issue and same width redraw in place; a different issue opens at line 0.

**Layout** (#2, variant E: paged). The detail pane takes `max(40% of width, 38)`. The board gets the rest. The number of columns shown is the most that fit at a minimum of 28 wide, between 1 and 4. The first visible column shifts so the focused column is always on screen, from either side. The board border title shows `◀ <hidden left> · <hidden right> ▶` when fewer than four columns fit. Columns are separated by a dim `│`. This geometry, trimmed from the prototype:

```go
// E: columns never go below minColW; what does not fit scrolls sideways,
// always keeping the focused column on screen. The detail pane yields to 40%.
const minColW = 28
detailOuter := max(width*2/5, 38)
boardW := max(width-detailOuter-2, 1)
n := max(1, min(4, (boardW+1)/(minColW+1)))
if col < first { first = col }
if col >= first+n { first = col - n + 1 }
first = max(0, min(first, 4-n))
if n < 4 { title += fmt.Sprintf(" · ◀ %d · %d ▶", first, 4-first-n) }
```

**Card** (3 lines; geometry lives in `tui`, like row geometry, with `render.Ellipsis`/`render.Cols`/`render.StatusMark` as the primitives):

1. `<mark> P<n> <type> <id>`, with the age flush right and the left side cut to fit. The age counts from `created_at` for Ready and Blocked, `started_at` for In progress, and `closed_at` for Closed.
2. The title, cut with an ellipsis.
3. The present parts joined with ` · `, then cut. Order of parts, trimmed from the prototype:

```go
if assignee != ""   { facts = append(facts, "@"+assignee) }
if blockedBy > 0    { facts = append(facts, fmt.Sprintf("blocked by %d", blockedBy)) }
if downstream > 0   { facts = append(facts, fmt.Sprintf("unblocks %d", downstream)) }
if len(labels) > 0  { facts = append(facts, "#"+strings.Join(labels, " #")) }
line3 := render.Ellipsis(strings.Join(facts, " · "), width)
```

Cards are separated by one blank line. The focused card, in the focused column only, is reverse video. The prototype also dims closed cards. The prototype's age buckets (`m` under an hour, `h` under 48 hours, `d` under 60 days, `mo` under a year, then `y`) are a reasonable default, and the clock must be a constructor-passed fact, not `time.Now()` at the point of use.

**Column heading.** `<name> <count>`. Only while the column overflows, append ` · <first>–<last>` (1-based, en dash). `▸ ` prefixes only the focused column, which is styled as a heading. Other columns get two spaces and are dimmed. An empty column shows a dim hint under its heading: `r to show blocked` for Blocked under `r`, `nothing closed` for Closed, and `none` otherwise. A column scrolls one card at a time so the cursor's card stays on screen.

**What the prototype is not.** It sorts Closed locally, reads labels once per card, and calls `OpenBlockers` twice. All three are exactly what the core changes above replace. It is throwaway and must not be merged. Take the look from it, not the structure.

**Contract** (#6). `docs/cli-contract.md`:
- Add a sentence to the navigator intro saying it has two views.
- Add `B`, `tab`, and `m` rows to the key table, and to the `?` help screen.
- Add a new `### The board` subsection at the end of "The navigator: `drops tui`". It says once that every key keeps its meaning, then lists the exceptions: the derived columns, the 3-line card, `tab`, `m` and its three flows, `C`'s notice, `r` emptying Blocked, where the cursor lands after a write, and paging.
- Add one **Known rough edges** line: Closed loads with no limit, and a refresh costs about 100ms at around 10k closed issues.
- Change nothing else, and add no exit code.
- `CHANGELOG.md`: add an entry under `## [Unreleased]` → Added.

## Testing Decisions

**What a good test is here.** It asserts behaviour a reader can observe, against real temp SQLite, through the highest seam available. That seam is the navigator's `Model`, driven by key messages from the existing `fixture` (`f.model(width, height)`), and core's public methods for the core changes. There are no fakes for the store. Discovered facts, the clock among them, are constructor parameters. Each requirement clause gets a catalogued mutation control that has been seen to go red (`just mutate`). A golden frame is not a control.

**Test levels**, all against real temp SQLite:
- **Model state after key messages:** column membership, the focused and first visible column, cursor landing, notices, and what `B` carries over.
- **Store effect**, re-read through the fixture: every `m` flow, with a real `sh` editor for close. Prior art: `editor_test.go` and `actions_test.go` (`editorLeaves`, `chooseRow`, `TestTheRoundTripClosesAnIssueThroughARealEditorProcess`).
- **Frames:** add board modes to `frameModes` at 80, 120, and 200 columns. They assert only that every line measures the frame width and the composed frame is square, as `frame_test.go` does. No saved snapshot frames, and they are not controls.
- **Byte-exact:** a card-render function covering all three card lines and the column heading. Prior art: `rows_test.go` (`TestRowAppendsTheBlockedMarkerAfterTheCut`, `TestIDColumnAutoSizesButCapsAtTwelve`).
- **Core:** prior art is `mutations_test.go` for the write and `graph_test.go` for the blocker graph.

**TUI controls** (`internal/tui/mutations.json`). Rule: controls go only on branches the board owns. Where the board calls a flow the list already has (the editor's two refusals, reopen's `y`, the `r` predicate, the poll and stale marker), it gets a test through the board path but no second control, unless it is a board branch that chooses which flow to run.

1. Column derivation, one control per branch: open + ready → Ready; open + blocked → Blocked; in progress + blocked → In progress; closed → Closed.
2. Closed order: the board does not re-sort.
3. `m` picker rows: the card's own status is left out; Ready and Blocked appear as one `open` row.
4. `m` → in progress calls start-and-claim, not `SetIssueStatus`.
5. `m` → closed goes through the editor flow. Leaving Closed goes through the reopen prompt, and only when there is a reason to lose.
6. `open — blocked by N` appears only when the card lands in Blocked.
7. Cursor after a write (three controls): it follows its id into the new column; if the card left, it goes to the next card, else the previous one, else the nearest non-empty column.
8. `tab` lands on the nearest row position and wraps around the four columns.
9. Paging (two controls): columns shown = max(1, board width ÷ 28), and the focused column scrolls into view from the left and from the right.
10. Card and heading: the age source depends on the column; each part of line 3 appears only when present; the range appears only on overflow; `▸` marks only the focused column.
11. Empty hints: `r to show blocked` only under `r` and only in Blocked; `nothing closed` only in Closed.
12. `C` shows its notice and leaves the list's `C` state alone (two controls). `B` reads nothing and carries the cursor id over.

"The cursor and card stay put after a cancelled close or declined reopen" gets a board-path test but no control, because existing controls already cover it.

**Core controls** (`internal/core/mutations.json`):
- Start-and-claim: claims only when unclaimed; leaves an existing claim alone; sets `started_at` only once; refuses a tombstoned issue.
- Closed read: `closed_at DESC`; `id` breaks ties; scoped to the project (all projects under `a`); closed only, tombstoned excluded.
- Live-labels read: tombstoned memberships excluded; names sorted.
- Blocker-graph read: the "only this blocker" downstream rule still holds when impacts come from a map the caller passes.
- "`OpenBlockers` is read once per refresh" is a cost, not a behaviour. Check it with a benchmark or a read count, and **do not catalogue** it.

Record each control, its red test, and the restore in the closing comment (`just mutate <package>` output). The gate is `just test-all`.

## Out of Scope

Carried over from the map:

- **Grouping modes** (bv's `s`: priority or type columns). Not v1. No new data is needed, so it's a TUI-only follow-up once v1 exists.
- **Manual ordering within a column.** It needs a rank column (schema v8) and a sync merge rule for a new replicated record. Priority already acts as the rank.
- **Custom workflow stages** (review, QA). A change to the three-status model that readiness and sync depend on; its own effort if ever.
- **A separate `drops board` command.** The board lives inside `drops tui`.
- **A CLI verb for the start-and-claim write** (e.g. `drops start`). It would change the agent-facing CLI contract, which is beyond this spec.
- **A test holding the `?` help screen to the contract's key table.** A new doc-sync test for the whole navigator, not something the board needs; its own ticket if wanted.

Also ruled out by the child tickets:

- A `--board` flag or opening `drops tui` in the board.
- `Esc` leaving the board.
- Releasing a claim on any move.
- An inline close-reason text box, or allowing an empty close reason.
- Separate Ready and Blocked targets in the move picker.
- A revision guard against what the board last displayed.
- A limit on the Closed read.
- A local sort of Closed in the TUI, per-card label reads, or TUI-side downstream counting.
- Any change to polling or the stale marker.
- bv's fourth card line (labels alone).
- The rejected layouts: four columns squeezed into the list's half, a focused column with collapsed strips, the board stacked above the detail pane, and a grouped list.
- Saved snapshot frames as tests.

## Further Notes

- **Scaling past the corpus** (the map's open question, not a v1 prerequisite): at 10k closed issues a board refresh is about 105ms, and the cost is in `OpenBlockers`, which reads every full issue row to learn which issues are terminal. The plain list pays the same. Revisit if a real store grows that large.
- Measured refresh costs (#4), 1,031 issues / 10,031 issues: open and in-progress `Issues` 0.15ms / 0.15ms; `Issues` including closed 4.2 / 54ms; `OpenBlockers` 4.1 / 48ms; `UnblockImpacts` 3.9 / 47ms; `store.Labels()` 0.33 / 3.2ms; whole board refresh **8.8ms / 105ms**.
- Read `internal/tui`'s `doc.go` before starting: the refresh/poll split, the follow stack, why the detail pane is opaque, and why `r` is a local predicate rather than `core.Ready`.
- The prototype runs with `just board-prototype` on its branch (`[` `]` switch layouts, `d` card lines, `<` `>` force the width). It seeds a scratch store through core's write path, and `-db <path>` points it at another store.
- Suggested order for `/to-tickets`: the four core changes first (independent of each other), then board mode in the TUI, then the contract and changelog.

## Problem Statement

`drops tui` shows one scope as a flat list, in the CLI's order. To see where the work stands (what can be picked up, what is waiting on something, what is under way, and what just finished), a person has to switch `r` and `C` on and off and hold the rest in their head. The list marks a blocked row with ` [N]` but cannot group rows by where they are in the flow. It also hides closed work unless `C` is on, and then mixes it in with live rows. Moving an issue along the flow means opening `x` and picking a verb, and there is no one motion that says "I'm starting this".

## Solution

A **board** view inside `drops tui`. `B` switches between the list and the board. The board sets out the live issues in scope in four derived **Board columns** (Ready | Blocked | In progress | Closed), one card per issue, with the detail pane still on screen to the right. `tab`/`shift+tab` moves between columns. Every existing key keeps its meaning. `m` moves a card by changing its status, using the flows the navigator already has for closing and reopening. Moving a card into In progress also claims it if nobody holds the claim, in one write.

At narrow widths the board shows as many columns as fit, each at least 28 wide, and scrolls sideways to keep the focused column on screen. Polling, the stale marker, follow, `x`, and `y` work as they do in the list.

## User Stories

**Entering, leaving, and what carries over**

1. As a person at a terminal, I want `B` to switch `drops tui` between the list and the board, so that I can see the flow without leaving the navigator.
2. As a person, I want `drops tui` to always open in the list, so that starting it behaves as it did before the board.
3. As a person, I want the issue under my cursor to stay the cursor's issue when I press `B`, so that switching views doesn't lose my place.
4. As a person, I want my `/` filter, `a` scope, `r` narrowing, and follow trail to carry over when I press `B`, so that the board narrows to what the list was narrowed to.
5. As a person, I want `B` to read nothing from the store, so that switching views is instant and the rows don't change under me.
6. As a person, I want `Esc` not to leave the board, so that a stray `Esc` while backing out of a picker or filter doesn't drop me into the list.
7. As a person who uses `b` to page the detail pane up, I want `b` to keep doing that, so that the board key doesn't take a key I already use.

**Columns**

8. As a person, I want open issues with no unfinished blocker in **Ready**, so that I can see what can be picked up.
9. As a person, I want open issues with at least one unfinished blocker in **Blocked**, so that I can see what is waiting.
10. As a person, I want every `in_progress` issue in **In progress**, even a blocked one, so that started work never looks unstarted.
11. As a person, I want a blocked In progress card to say `blocked by N`, so that I can see started work that is stuck.
12. As a person, I want closed issues in **Closed**, always shown whatever `C` is set to, so that recently finished work is on the board.
13. As a person, I want Closed ordered most recently closed first, so that the top of the column is what just finished.
14. As a person, I want Ready, Blocked, and In progress in the CLI's order (priority, newest, id), so that the board and `drops list` agree.
15. As a person, I want no manual ranking, so that priority stays the one ordering tool.
16. As a person, I want tombstoned issues never to appear on the board, so that removed work doesn't clutter it.

**Cards**

17. As a person, I want line 1 of a card to show the status mark, `P<n>`, type, and id, with age right-aligned, so that I can identify a card at a glance.
18. As a person, I want a card's age measured from when it was created (Ready and Blocked), started (In progress), or closed (Closed), so that the age means something in each column.
19. As a person, I want line 2 to be the title, cut with an ellipsis, so that long titles don't break the column.
20. As a person, I want line 3 to show `@assignee · blocked by N · unblocks N · #label #label`, with each part only when present, so that I see who holds it, what it waits on, what it frees, and how it's tagged, without empty placeholders.
21. As a person, I want a card's labels to be its live labels only, so that removed labels don't show.
22. As a person, I want one blank line between cards and the focused card in reverse video, so that cards read as separate and I can see which is selected.

**Layout and width**

23. As a person, I want the detail pane to stay on screen at 40% of the frame (at least 38 columns), so that the page for the focused card is always readable.
24. As a person on an 80-column terminal, I want one full-width column at a time rather than four unreadable slivers, so that cards stay legible.
25. As a person at 120 columns, I want two columns, and at 200 columns all four, so that wider terminals show more of the board.
26. As a person, I want the board border to say how many columns are hidden on each side (e.g. `◀ 1 · 1 ▶`), so that I know there is more off screen.

37. As a person, I want `h` `l` `←` `→` `0` `$` `J` `K` `space` `b` `w` `enter` `f` `Backspace` `x` `y` to act on the detail pane as they do in the list, so that I don't learn a second keymap.

38. As a person, I want `/` to filter the cards in every column, so that filtering works the same in both views.
39. As a person, I want `r` on the board to use the same ready-only predicate as the list, so that "ready" means one thing.
40. As a person, I want Blocked to show `r to show blocked` while `r` is on, so that I know why it's empty and how to get it back.

42. As a person, I want `C` on the board to show the notice `closed always shown on the board`, cleared by the next key, so that I know the key did nothing on purpose.

45. As a person, I want the picker to leave out the card's current status, so that every row changes something.
46. As a person, I want Ready and Blocked to appear as one `open` row, so that I'm not offered a column the card might not land in.
47. As a person, I want a card moved to `open` to land in whichever of Ready or Blocked its readiness puts it, so that columns stay derived.
48. As a person, I want a status line (e.g. `open — blocked by 2`) when a card moved to `open` lands in Blocked, so that I know why it didn't land in Ready.
49. As a person, I want moving a card into In progress to claim it for me if nobody holds the claim, so that starting work and taking it are one motion.
50. As a person, I want moving into In progress to leave someone else's claim alone and still succeed, so that I can mark work started without taking it from its owner.
51. As a person, I want `started_at` set only the first time an issue enters In progress, so that the start date isn't reset by moving a card back and forth.
52. As a person, I want moving out of In progress never to release the claim, so that a move never drops ownership by accident (`x release` still does that).
53. As a person, I want moving a card to `closed` to open the same `$EDITOR` flow as `x close`, so that every close has a written reason.
54. As a person, I want an empty or whitespace-only reason, or a non-zero editor exit, to cancel the close and leave the card where it was, so that I can back out.
55. As a person, I want closing not to touch the claim, so that the claim records who resolved the issue.
56. As a person, I want moving a card out of Closed to ask the same y/N as `reopen`, including how many characters of close reason will be lost, so that I don't lose a reason by accident.
57. As a person, I want no prompt when a closed issue has no close reason, so that there's no confirmation when nothing is lost.
58. As a person, I want any answer but `y` to leave the card in Closed, so that a stray key never reopens anything.
59. As a person, I want moving a card from Closed to In progress to ask the reopen question and then claim if unclaimed, so that both rules apply in order.

60. As a person, I want the cursor to follow a moved card into whichever column it lands in, so that I can keep acting on it.
61. As a person, I want the cursor, if the card leaves the view (tombstoned, filtered out, or hidden by `r`), to go to the next card in its column, else the previous one, else the nearest non-empty column, so that I always land somewhere sensible.
